intervals.name: Near Future
intervals.summary: Continents still roughly modern in outline; East Africa fully rifts off and Australia drives north into Asia. Solar output is only about 0.3% above today, so brightening is negligible and global temperature is set by geography and the carbon cycle, not the Sun. The biosphere is essentially intact — mammals, plants, marine and microbial life all thriving — with only a modest expansion of subtropical drylands as the first hint of the supercontinent to come.
key_events: +2 Myr — Afar rift floods; the Red Sea joins the East African Rift
+10 Myr — Australia's leading edge collides with the Indonesian arc
+15 Myr — Los Angeles draws level with San Francisco
+20 Myr — the Mediterranean has narrowed by roughly 200 km
+30 Myr — Atlantic about 1,000 km wider; Pacific correspondingly smaller

intervals.name: Mediterranean Closure
intervals.summary: Africa collides with Europe and the Mediterranean is squeezed shut, welding Africa and Arabia to Eurasia and raising a new Alpine-scale range. Solar luminosity is up about half a percent, still a minor forcing. Growing continental interiority amplifies seasonal extremes and widens the desert belts; life stays broadly modern, but heat- and drought-stressed mammal ranges begin to fragment across the enlarging arid interior.
key_events: +35 Myr — the Mediterranean is reduced to isolated saline remnants
+50 Myr — Afro-European collision belt reaches full height
+50 Myr — Australia fully sutured to Southeast Asia
+60 Myr — Gibraltar-type subduction either takes hold in the Atlantic or does not
+80 Myr — Atlantic near its maximum width, roughly 3,000 km wider than today

intervals.name: Atlantic Reversal
intervals.summary: The Atlantic stops widening and begins to close as new subduction zones consume its floor, pulling the Americas back toward Eurasia and Africa. Solar brightening reaches about one percent and CO2 climbs as assembly-stage volcanism outpaces silicate weathering. A genuinely hot, arid supercontinental interior takes shape; vegetation retreats toward coasts and highlands and mammal habitability contracts markedly — though plants, marine and microbial life stay abundant.
key_events: +90 Myr — subduction propagates north and south from the Caribbean arc
+100 Myr — oldest Atlantic crust exceeds 200 Myr and begins to founder
+120 Myr — Atlantic spreading ceases; the basin starts to close
+140 Myr — the Americas' motion reverses from westward to eastward

intervals.name: Proxima Assembly
intervals.summary: The landmasses coalesce into a near-complete supercontinent ringed by one great ocean. Solar output is roughly 1.3 to 1.9 percent above present and elevated CO2 keeps the planet warm; the interior becomes lethally hot and hyper-arid. Mammalian habitable land shrinks toward the Farnsworth range, life is forced poleward and onto coastal and upland refugia, and the complex land-animal biosphere approaches its tipping point — while the ocean and microbial worlds are barely touched.
key_events: +160 Myr — the Atlantic is reduced to a narrow interior seaway
+170 Myr — Neo-Himalayan belt rises as the last Tethyan crust is consumed
+180 Myr — Antarctica clears the South Pole and moves into temperate latitudes
+200 Myr — continental interiors pass 2,000 km from the nearest coast; aridity climbs

intervals.name: Pangaea Proxima
intervals.summary: Full assembly of Pangaea Proxima (Pangaea Ultima). Solar luminosity is about 2.5 percent above today and background CO2 sits in the 400 to 800 ppm range: global mean near 24 C, land-only 29 to 30 C, with monthly interior heat above 50 C exceeding the dry- and wet-bulb limits of mammals. Only 8 to 16 percent of land stays habitable for them (against about 66 percent now), so complex land animals face probable mass extinction. Crucially the planet is NOT lifeless: heat-restricted vegetation survives on margins and highlands, and marine and microbial life remain abundant — true biosphere-wide collapse still lies 0.5 to 2.8 billion years further ahead, with solar-driven CO2 starvation and ocean loss.
key_events: +220 Myr — the Atlantic closes; Trans-Atlantic suture completed
+230 Myr — a Himalayan-scale range runs the length of the new suture
+240 Myr — the trapped Indian Ocean becomes an inland sea
+250 Myr — solar luminosity ~2.5% above present; modelled interiors reach 40-50 C

intervals.name: Quaternary
intervals.summary: The shortest period on the chart and the only one defined by a climate event: its base at 2.58 Ma marks the point at which Northern Hemisphere ice sheets became a permanent fixture rather than an occasional one. Tectonically almost nothing changes at this timescale — the Himalaya, Andes and Alps keep rising, the Atlantic keeps widening a few centimetres a year — so the story is entirely climatic and biological. Ice sheets advanced and retreated on a 41,000-year obliquity beat until the Mid-Pleistocene Transition between roughly 1.25 and 0.7 Ma, after which the rhythm switched to a sawtooth 100,000-year cycle with far larger ice volumes. Sea level swung through about 130 metres with each cycle, exposing and drowning continental shelves, opening and closing Beringia and the Sunda shelf. Homo erectus, Neanderthals and Homo sapiens all appear within this period, and the large-bodied mammal faunas of every continent except Africa collapse near its end. The Holocene, everything since 11,700 years ago, is the current interglacial.
key_events: 2.58 Ma — Northern Hemisphere ice sheets become permanent; Quaternary begins
1.9 Ma — Homo erectus, the first hominin to leave Africa
1.25-0.7 Ma — Mid-Pleistocene Transition; glacial cycles shift from 41 kyr to 100 kyr
~300 ka — earliest Homo sapiens, Jebel Irhoud, Morocco
20 ka — Last Glacial Maximum; sea level 125-130 m below present
11.7 ka — Holocene begins; ice sheets retreat, sea level rises ~120 m

intervals.name: Pliocene
intervals.summary: The Pliocene opens with the most spectacular flood in the geological record: at 5.33 Ma the Atlantic breached the Gibraltar sill and refilled a Mediterranean that had spent the previous 600,000 years as a desiccating salt desert two kilometres below sea level. The Isthmus of Panama completed a land bridge during this epoch, letting North and South American mammals invade each other's continents and reorganising ocean circulation. Shoaling had been under way since perhaps 10 Ma and the CLOSURE DATE is actively debated; what is well dated is the interchange, which accelerates sharply at about 2.7 Ma. The mid-Piacenzian warm period between about 3.3 and 3.0 Ma is the closest well-documented analogue for the near-future climate: CO2 around 350 to 450 ppm, global temperature 2 to 3 C above pre-industrial, and sea level 10 to 25 metres higher than today with the same continental geometry. Then it cooled: the Greenland ice sheet became permanent around 2.7 Ma. C4 grasslands continued spreading, Australopithecus walked upright across East African savanna, the first members of the genus Homo appear near 2.8 Ma, and the largest shark that ever lived, Otodus megalodon, went extinct.
key_events: 5.33 Ma — Zanclean flood refills the desiccated Mediterranean in as little as two years
4.5-2.8 Ma — Isthmus of Panama completes a land bridge (closure date debated); Great American Biotic Interchange begins
3.6 Ma — Otodus megalodon extinct
3.3-3.0 Ma — mid-Piacenzian warm period; sea level 10-25 m above present
3.2 Ma — 'Lucy', Australopithecus afarensis, Hadar, Ethiopia
2.7 Ma — Greenland ice sheet becomes permanent

intervals.name: Miocene
intervals.summary: The longest Cenozoic epoch, and the one in which the modern world becomes recognisable. Arabia collided with Eurasia around 20 Ma, finally severing the Tethyan seaway that had circled the tropics since the Mesozoic and opening a land bridge that let elephants walk into Eurasia and apes walk into Africa. The Alps and Himalaya rose hard, the Red Sea began to open, the East African Rift tore southward, and the Columbia River Basalts flooded the Pacific Northwest around 16 Ma. Climate peaked in the Miocene Climatic Optimum between 17 and 14.7 Ma, then fell off a cliff at the Middle Miocene Climate Transition as the East Antarctic ice sheet expanded to something close to its modern volume. The epoch ends with the Messinian Salinity Crisis: between 5.97 and 5.33 Ma tectonic closure of the Gibraltar gateway evaporated the Mediterranean, leaving over a million cubic kilometres of salt beneath its floor. Grasslands and C4 photosynthesis expanded worldwide after about 8 Ma, driving the radiation of high-crowned grazing mammals, and the hominin and chimpanzee lineages separated near 7 Ma.
key_events: 20 Ma — Arabia docks with Eurasia; the Tethyan seaway is severed
17-14.7 Ma — Miocene Climatic Optimum
16 Ma — Columbia River Basalts erupt as the Yellowstone plume arrives
14 Ma — Middle Miocene Climate Transition; East Antarctic ice sheet expands
~7 Ma — hominin and chimpanzee lineages diverge
5.97-5.33 Ma — Messinian Salinity Crisis; the Mediterranean dries out

intervals.name: Oligocene
intervals.summary: The epoch in which Earth switched from a greenhouse world to the icehouse it still inhabits. At 33.9 Ma, over a few hundred thousand years, atmospheric CO2 fell below roughly 700 ppm and a continental ice sheet formed on East Antarctica for the first time in more than 200 million years — the Oi-1 event, recorded worldwide as a step in benthic oxygen isotopes. The trigger was partly tectonic: the Tasman Gateway and Drake Passage opened as Australia and South America cleared Antarctica, allowing the Antarctic Circumpolar Current to close the loop and thermally isolate the continent. Sea level dropped 50 to 70 metres as water was locked into ice, exposing shelves worldwide. On land, Europe's endemic mammal fauna was replaced almost wholesale by Asian immigrants in the turnover known as the Grande Coupure. Open woodland and early grassland spread, the enormous hornless rhinoceros Paraceratherium browsed across central Asia, and the baleen and toothed whale lineages separated in the newly cold, productive Southern Ocean.
key_events: 33.9 Ma — Eocene-Oligocene Transition; first permanent East Antarctic ice sheet
33.9 Ma — Grande Coupure: European mammal faunas replaced by Asian immigrants
~33 Ma — sea level falls 50-70 m as ice volume grows
30 Ma — Ethiopian Traps erupt; the Afar plume domes East Africa
~30 Ma — Antarctic Circumpolar Current established as Drake Passage deepens
25 Ma — East African Rift begins to open

intervals.name: Eocene
intervals.summary: The hottest sustained interval of the last 66 million years. During the Early Eocene Climatic Optimum, roughly 53 to 49 Ma, global mean temperature reached about 26 to 27 C — some 12 C above today — with no permanent ice anywhere on the planet, crocodilians and palms on Ellesmere Island at 78 degrees north, and Arctic Ocean surface waters near 23 C. India, having crossed Tethys faster than any continent known, made contact with Asia between about 55 and 50 Ma and began raising the Himalaya; meanwhile Greenland tore away from Europe and the North Atlantic opened. Cooling then ran almost continuously for the rest of the epoch, helped near 49 Ma by the Azolla event, in which a freshwater fern bloomed across a stagnant Arctic basin and buried enough carbon to matter. Every modern mammal order with a hoof, a hand or a fin appears here: the first horses, the first primates of modern aspect, and the whale lineage's whole transition from the wading Pakicetus to the fully aquatic Basilosaurus. The late Eocene also carries a cluster of large impacts, including Popigai and Chesapeake Bay within about a million years of each other.
key_events: 56 Ma — Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum; 5-8 C warming in under 20,000 years
55-50 Ma — India makes contact with Asia; Himalayan building begins
53-49 Ma — Early Eocene Climatic Optimum, the Cenozoic's warmest interval
49 Ma — Azolla event: fern blooms across a fresh-capped Arctic Ocean
~40 Ma — Basilosaurus, fully aquatic whales, in the Tethys seaway
35.7-34.9 Ma — Popigai and Chesapeake Bay impacts, a late Eocene cluster

intervals.name: Paleocene
intervals.summary: Ten million years of recovery, bracketed by two of the sharpest carbon events in the record. It opens in the immediate aftermath of Chicxulub and the Deccan Traps, with a world stripped of non-avian dinosaurs, ammonites, mosasaurs and most plankton; the boundary clay is followed everywhere by a 'fern spike', the signature of a disturbed landscape recolonised by opportunists. Mammals, which had spent 100 million years small and nocturnal, radiated into the vacated large-body niches within a few million years, and tropical rainforest of modern structure appears for the first time. Tectonically, Greenland and Europe were pulling apart with the North Atlantic Igneous Province erupting along the rift, India was still racing north, and the Laramide orogeny was thickening western North America far inland from the plate margin. The epoch ends at 56 Ma with the Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum: a release of thousands of gigatonnes of carbon that warmed the planet 5 to 8 C in under 20,000 years, acidified the deep ocean and wiped out a large fraction of benthic foraminifera — the closest geological parallel to the present carbon release, and still roughly ten times slower.
key_events: 66.05 Ma — Chicxulub impact ends the Cretaceous; Deccan Traps still erupting
66 Ma — global 'fern spike' marks the devastated post-impact landscape
~64 Ma — placental mammals radiate into vacated large-bodied niches
~62 Ma — Cerrejon rainforest, Colombia: Titanoboa, a 13 m snake
61 Ma — North Atlantic Igneous Province peaks as Greenland parts from Europe
56 Ma — Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum; benthic foraminiferal extinction

intervals.name: Late Cretaceous
intervals.summary: The high-water mark of the Phanerozoic, in every sense. Sea level stood 170 to 250 metres above present — the highest of the last 540 million years — because fast seafloor spreading kept the ocean ridges hot, young and voluminous, displacing water onto the continents. Shallow seas split North America from the Arctic to the Gulf, flooded central Australia and North Africa, and laid down the coccolith ooze that became the chalk of Dover and Champagne. Global mean temperature peaked near 30 C in the Turonian, around 92 to 90 Ma, with no ice at either pole and ocean anoxic event OAE2 blacking out the seafloor at 94 Ma. Gondwana came apart: Madagascar and India separated around 88 Ma, the South Atlantic fully opened, and the Sevier-Laramide orogeny built western North America. Angiosperms went from newcomers to dominant, co-radiating with bees and other pollinators, while rudist bivalves displaced corals as the main reef builders. It ends abruptly at 66.05 Ma, when a ten-kilometre asteroid struck a sulphate-rich Yucatan shelf and the Deccan Traps were mid-eruption.
key_events: 100.5 Ma — Late Cretaceous begins; sea level rising toward its Phanerozoic maximum
94 Ma — Ocean Anoxic Event 2; widespread seafloor anoxia and black shale
92-90 Ma — Cretaceous Thermal Maximum; global mean temperature near 30 C
88 Ma — Madagascar separates from India; Madagascar Traps erupt
~68 Ma — Tyrannosaurus and Triceratops in western North America
66.05 Ma — Chicxulub impact; ~75% of species extinct, all non-avian dinosaurs

intervals.name: Early Cretaceous
intervals.summary: Gondwana tore in half. The Parana-Etendeka basalts erupted at 134 Ma across what is now Brazil and Namibia, and the South Atlantic unzipped northward behind them between about 134 and 112 Ma, one province split into two continents. Simultaneously the Ontong Java Plateau erupted onto the Pacific floor at 122 Ma — the largest single volcanic edifice on Earth, emplaced in perhaps a few million years — pushing the mid-Cretaceous toward its greenhouse extreme. The epoch opened cool, with the timeline's only Mesozoic hint of polar ice around the Jurassic-Cretaceous boundary, then warmed steadily; the Valanginian Weissert event at about 135 Ma is the first of the epoch's carbon cycle disturbances. Sea level climbed throughout. Biologically this is the epoch that made the modern land: flowering plants appear in the fossil record around 130 to 125 Ma and diversify explosively, while the ash-buried Jehol Biota of northeastern China preserves feathered dinosaurs, early birds and early placental mammals in enough detail to show individual filaments and, in some specimens, melanosomes that give the original colour.
key_events: 143.1 Ma — Cretaceous begins after a cool snap at the Jurassic boundary
135 Ma — Weissert event, a major carbon-cycle perturbation
134 Ma — Parana-Etendeka basalts erupt; the South Atlantic begins to open
~130-125 Ma — first unambiguous flowering plants (Archaefructus, Montsechia)
125 Ma — Jehol Biota: feathered dinosaurs, early birds, early mammals
122 Ma — Ontong Java Plateau, the largest oceanic plateau on Earth

intervals.name: Late Jurassic
intervals.summary: Pangaea was now unambiguously two continents: Laurasia in the north, Gondwana in the south, with Tethys opening eastward between them and the young Central Atlantic widening in the west. Sea level was high and warm epicontinental seas covered much of Europe and interior North America, producing two of the most productive fossil deposits ever found — the Solnhofen lagoons of Bavaria, whose oxygen-starved lime mud preserved Archaeopteryx and countless soft-bodied animals, and the Morrison Formation of the American West. No ice existed at either pole and global mean temperature sat around 22 to 23 C. This is the interval of maximum sauropod: Brachiosaurus, Diplodocus, Apatosaurus and Camarasaurus in North America, Giraffatitan in Tanzania, all hunted by Allosaurus and Ceratosaurus. In the sea, ammonites and belemnites were at their most diverse, ichthyosaurs and plesiosaurs cruised the shelves, and coral reefs rebuilt on a scale not seen since the Triassic. Mammals remained small, nocturnal and inconspicuous throughout.
key_events: 161.5 Ma — Late Jurassic begins; Laurasia and Gondwana now fully separate
~155 Ma — Morrison Formation: Diplodocus, Brachiosaurus, Allosaurus
~150 Ma — Solnhofen lagoons; Archaeopteryx, the first known bird
~150 Ma — Sundance Sea floods western North America from the Arctic
146 Ma — Morokweng impact, 70 km crater, southern Africa
145 Ma — cool interval near the Jurassic-Cretaceous boundary; possible polar ice

intervals.name: Middle Jurassic
intervals.summary: A quiet, warm, wet interval that gets less attention than it deserves, because it is when the Atlantic actually started. True seafloor spreading began in the Central Atlantic around 170 Ma, some thirty million years after the CAMP eruptions cracked Pangaea open; before that the rift had been floored by salt and continental crust, and the thick evaporites now buried beneath the Gulf of Mexico date from that transitional phase. Tethys spread westward to link with the new ocean, giving a circum-equatorial current for the first time in the Mesozoic. Climate was warm, humid and unusually equable, with no ice and few extremes, and sea level rose strongly from the Toarcian lowstand. Dinosaurs consolidated their dominance and sauropods reached genuinely enormous size for the first time. Mammals split into the lineages leading to marsupials and placentals during this epoch, and the earliest known gliding and swimming mammals both come from Middle Jurassic rocks in China. Megalosaurus, from the Bathonian of Oxfordshire, was in 1824 the first dinosaur ever formally named.
key_events: 174.7 Ma — Middle Jurassic begins; strong marine transgression after the Toarcian
~170 Ma — seafloor spreading begins in the Central Atlantic
~168 Ma — Megalosaurus, later the first dinosaur ever named, in Oxfordshire
~165 Ma — marsupial and placental mammal lineages diverge
~164 Ma — Volaticotherium and Castorocauda: gliding and swimming Jurassic mammals

intervals.name: Early Jurassic
intervals.summary: Opens in catastrophe and closes in abundance. The Central Atlantic Magmatic Province erupted across four future continents at 201 Ma, releasing enough CO2 to acidify the oceans and drive the end-Triassic mass extinction, which removed about three quarters of species and cleared the last serious competitors to the dinosaurs. Recovery was fast in the sea: ammonites, reduced to a handful of surviving lineages, re-radiated so rapidly and so distinctively that they became the finest biostratigraphic tool in the entire geological record, dividing the epoch into zones of under a million years. Marine transgression flooded the continents, and the resulting black shales at Lyme Regis and Holzmaden preserve ichthyosaurs with skin outlines and unborn young — the deposits Mary Anning quarried, which gave the nineteenth century its first real evidence of extinct worlds. The Toarcian Oceanic Anoxic Event at about 183 Ma, coincident with the Karoo-Ferrar eruptions that were beginning to split Gondwana, brought another sharp warming and a second pulse of seafloor anoxia.
key_events: 201.4 Ma — end-Triassic extinction; CAMP eruptions crack Pangaea open
~199 Ma — ammonites re-radiate from a few surviving lineages
~195 Ma — Lyme Regis and Holzmaden shales; ichthyosaurs and plesiosaurs
194 Ma — Puchezh-Katunki impact, 40 km crater on the Russian platform
183 Ma — Karoo-Ferrar eruptions and Toarcian Oceanic Anoxic Event

intervals.name: Late Triassic
intervals.summary: Pangaea was still intact but under tension, its eastern seaboard cracking into the rift valleys — the Newark basins of New Jersey and Connecticut among them — that would become the Atlantic. The supercontinent's size drove a megamonsoon: violently seasonal, with an arid interior and wet margins. That pattern broke for about two million years during the Carnian Pluvial Episode, between roughly 234 and 232 Ma, when a sustained humid interval — most likely triggered by the Wrangellia eruptions — brought rain to the continental interior, restored peat-forming forests after the long Permian coal gap, and coincides with the first real diversification of dinosaurs. The first mammals appear near 225 Ma, shrew-sized and almost certainly nocturnal; pterosaurs took to the air, and the first true turtles and crocodile-line archosaurs appear. Manicouagan struck Quebec at 215.6 Ma leaving a 100 km crater. The epoch ends at 201.4 Ma with the end-Triassic extinction and the CAMP eruptions, which killed off the crocodile-line reptiles that had been the dinosaurs' main rivals.
key_events: 237 Ma — Late Triassic begins; Pangaea's megamonsoon at full strength
234-232 Ma — Carnian Pluvial Episode; dinosaurs begin to diversify
229 Ma — Wrangellia oceanic plateau erupts in Panthalassa
~225 Ma — first mammals (Adelobasileus, Morganucodon)
215.6 Ma — Manicouagan impact, 100 km crater in Quebec
201.4 Ma — end-Triassic extinction; ~75% of species lost

intervals.name: Middle Triassic
intervals.summary: Pangaea reached its most coherent configuration, a single C-shaped mass from pole to pole with Tethys biting into its eastern flank. Behind that gulf the Cimmerian terranes, rifted off Gondwana in the Permian, were drifting north, closing Palaeo-Tethys ahead of them and opening Neotethys behind. Climate was hot and arid, though no longer lethally so, and sea level was low but rising from the Early Triassic minimum. This is the interval when the biosphere finally finished recovering from the end-Permian catastrophe, some five to eight million years after the event. Reefs returned, built for the first time by scleractinian corals — the group that still builds them today — and the sea filled with newly evolved reptiles that had gone back to the water: nothosaurs, shell-crushing placodonts, long-necked Tanystropheus, and ichthyosaurs that reached whale scale within a few million years. On land the archosaurs split into the lineages leading to crocodiles and to dinosaurs, and Nyasasaurus from Tanzania, at about 245 Ma, may be the oldest dinosaur or its immediate sister.
key_events: 246.7 Ma — Middle Triassic begins; end-Permian recovery accelerates
~245 Ma — Nyasasaurus, possibly the oldest known dinosaur or its closest relative
~244 Ma — Monte San Giorgio marine reptile fauna: nothosaurs, Tanystropheus
~240 Ma — first scleractinian corals; modern-style reefs return
~239 Ma — the coal gap finally ends as peat-forming plants recover
~237 Ma — Cymbospondylus reaches whale scale barely 8 Myr after the extinction

intervals.name: Early Triassic
intervals.summary: Five million years in the worst world of the Phanerozoic. The Siberian Traps were still finishing, CO2 and temperature were at Phanerozoic highs, and equatorial sea surface temperatures reached about 40 C — hot enough that a band around the equator appears to have been essentially emptied of fish and tetrapods, the so-called equatorial tetrapod gap. There were no reefs anywhere on Earth for several million years and no coal anywhere for close to ten, because every peat-forming plant lineage had gone extinct: the most complete biome collapse in the plant fossil record. Land vertebrate faunas were reduced to near-monocultures, with the dicynodont Lystrosaurus accounting for something like 90 percent of tetrapod fossils across the whole planet — an animal found from Antarctica to Russia, which is itself a demonstration of how thoroughly Pangaea was joined. Recovery kept stalling, interrupted by repeated carbon-cycle swings, notably the Smithian-Spathian crisis around 249 Ma. Ichthyosaurs did appear early, by about 248 Ma, showing how quickly some lineages exploited the emptied ocean.
key_events: 251.902 Ma — Permian-Triassic boundary; the largest extinction in Earth history
~251 Ma — global coal gap begins; no peat-forming plants remain
~250 Ma — Lystrosaurus makes up ~90% of tetrapod fossils worldwide
~250 Ma — equatorial sea surface temperatures reach ~40 C; tropical tetrapod gap
~249 Ma — Smithian-Spathian crisis stalls the recovery
~248 Ma — first ichthyosaurs return reptiles to the sea

intervals.name: Late Permian (Lopingian)
intervals.summary: Pangaea was complete, the Urals had finished rising, and the supercontinent's interior was among the driest landscapes Earth has produced; the Zechstein Sea of northern Europe repeatedly flooded and evaporated, leaving the salt beds now buried beneath the North Sea. Sea level was low, continental area was at a maximum, and atmospheric oxygen was falling from its Palaeozoic peak. On land the therapsids ruled: sabre-toothed gorgonopsians hunting across Karoo floodplains, dicynodonts grazing in herds, and the first cynodonts — the lineage that leads to mammals. Gondwana was covered by Glossopteris forests, a seed-fern flora so distinctive that its presence across South America, Africa, India, Australia and Antarctica became one of the founding arguments for continental drift. Then, at 251.902 Ma, the Siberian Traps erupted through Siberian coal and evaporite, and the resulting carbon and sulphur load acidified the ocean, stripped it of oxygen and drove global temperature up roughly 8 to 10 C. About 81 percent of marine species and some 70 percent of terrestrial vertebrate genera vanished. Trilobites, which had survived for 270 million years, did not.
key_events: 259.51 Ma — Lopingian begins after the Capitanian extinction
~255 Ma — Glossopteris forests blanket Gondwana; peak Karoo therapsid diversity
254.7 Ma — Araguainha impact, Brazil's largest crater
~253 Ma — Zechstein Sea repeatedly evaporates, laying down North Sea salt
252 Ma — Siberian Traps erupt: ~4 million km3 of lava through coal and evaporite
251.902 Ma — end-Permian extinction; 81% of marine species die, trilobites gone

intervals.name: Middle Permian (Guadalupian)
intervals.summary: Pangaea's assembly was essentially finished and the Late Palaeozoic Ice Age was in its final act, the last Gondwanan ice sheets melting away during this epoch. Atmospheric oxygen stood at its Phanerozoic maximum, near 30 percent — 35 percent is the high end of older GEOCARBSULF runs, and Krause et al. (2022), the current review, sits at the lower figure — high enough that combustion behaviour and arthropod respiration both differed measurably from today. The Capitan Reef complex grew along the margin of the Delaware Basin in what is now west Texas and New Mexico, built not by corals but by sponges, algae and bryozoans, and now exhumed as the Guadalupe Mountains — one of the best-exposed ancient reefs on Earth. Therapsids dominated the land: bulky dinocephalians early, then dicynodonts, with the first true carnivorous gorgonopsians appearing. In the sea fusulinid foraminifera reached the size of wheat grains and became the epoch's index fossils. It closed with the Capitanian extinction at about 259.5 Ma, an event coincident with the Emeishan Traps of South China that removed a large fraction of marine genera some eight million years before the far greater end-Permian crisis.
key_events: 274.4 Ma — Guadalupian begins; last Gondwanan ice sheets in retreat
~270 Ma — atmospheric oxygen near its Phanerozoic maximum, ~30%
~265 Ma — Capitan Reef builds along the Delaware Basin margin
~262 Ma — dinocephalians give way to dicynodonts and gorgonopsians
260 Ma — Emeishan Traps erupt in South China
259.5 Ma — Capitanian (end-Guadalupian) extinction

intervals.name: Early Permian (Cisuralian)
intervals.summary: The ice went away. Gondwana's ice sheets, which had waxed and waned across the southern continents for some 60 million years, retreated through this epoch and were essentially gone by around 290 to 280 Ma, ending the Late Palaeozoic Ice Age — the longest icehouse of the Phanerozoic and the only one for which we have a detailed record of a fully glaciated Earth with forests and complex land animals already in place. Pangaea was welded together, the Urals were still rising along the Siberia-Laurussia suture, and the Panjal Traps at 289 Ma began rifting the Cimmerian terranes off Gondwana, opening Neotethys behind them. As the ice left, the world dried: red beds and evaporites spread, and the waterlogged lycopsid coal swamps of the Carboniferous were replaced by conifers, seed ferns and other drought-tolerant plants with proper reproductive independence from standing water. This is the world of the sail-backed pelycosaurs — Dimetrodon and the herbivorous Edaphosaurus — which are not dinosaurs but early synapsids, on our own side of the amniote split, and which gave way to the first therapsids before the epoch ended.
key_events: 298.9 Ma — Permian begins; Gondwanan ice sheets still extensive
297 Ma — Skagerrak-Centred magmatism as post-collisional Pangaea extends
~295 Ma — Dimetrodon and Edaphosaurus on Texas red-bed floodplains
~290 Ma — Late Palaeozoic Ice Age ends; Gondwanan ice essentially gone
289 Ma — Panjal Traps rift Cimmeria from Gondwana; Neotethys opens
~280 Ma — conifers and seed ferns replace lycopsid swamps as the world dries

intervals.name: Pennsylvanian
intervals.summary: Gondwana drove into Laurussia and Pangaea was assembled, throwing up the Central Pangaean Mountains — a Himalayan-scale range running from what is now Appalachia through Iberia into central Europe, preserved today as the Appalachian, Variscan and Ouachita belts. It happened during the peak of the Late Palaeozoic Ice Age, so sea level swung through more than a hundred metres on glacial cycles, repeatedly drowning and exposing the tropical coastal lowlands and stacking them into cyclothems: coal, shale, limestone, sandstone, repeat. Those coastal swamps were forests of lycopsids up to 40 metres tall — Lepidodendron, Sigillaria — with Calamites horsetails and tree ferns, and their burial is why this single period supplies so much of the world's coal. High atmospheric oxygen, around 30 percent, is the usual explanation for arthropods of a size never repeated: the millipede relative Arthropleura reached two and a half metres, and the dragonfly-like Meganeura had a 70 cm wingspan. That chain is a hypothesis rather than a settled result: both Arthropleura and Meganeura are now found in strata YOUNGER than the rainforest collapse, and both were probably forest-independent, so “high oxygen made them and the collapse killed them” is a story the fossil record does not yet support end to end. The first amniotes — vertebrates laying eggs that did not need water — appear near 318 Ma, and around 305 Ma the Carboniferous Rainforest Collapse fragmented the swamp forests into refugia and pushed the surviving tetrapods toward drier ground. The classic reading is that each surviving rainforest island then evolved its own fauna; a 2018 re-analysis found the opposite, increased COSMOPOLITANISM, so treat the fragmentation as established and its biogeographic consequence as open. The collapse is also Euramerican: the Cathaysian rainforests of South China persist to the end-Permian.

~318 Ma — Hylonomus, among the first amniotes, in Nova Scotian tree stumps
~315 Ma — peak coal-swamp forests; Lepidodendron reaches 40 m
~310 Ma — Arthropleura (2.5 m) and Meganeura (70 cm wingspan) under ~30% oxygen
~305 Ma — Carboniferous Rainforest Collapse fragments the tropical swamps
~300 Ma — Central Pangaean Mountains at full height; glacial cyclothems at maximum

intervals.name: Mississippian
intervals.summary: The transition from the Devonian greenhouse into the Late Palaeozoic Ice Age. Land plants had spent the Devonian rooting deeply into rock, accelerating silicate weathering and burying organic carbon; the CO2 drawdown finally caught up, and ice sheets began forming on Gondwana around 330 Ma. Before that, warm shallow seas spread across Laurussia and deposited some of the most extensive carbonate platforms in the record — limestone made so overwhelmingly of crinoid fragments that this is sometimes called the age of crinoids, with meadows of stalked echinoderms covering the seafloor. The Rheic Ocean was closing as Gondwana approached Laurussia, and on the far side of the continent the Antler orogeny thrust an island arc onto western Laurentia. Sharks radiated spectacularly into forms with no modern counterpart, including the brush-and-anvil-headed Stethacanthus. Most importantly, this epoch closes Romer's Gap: after a 15-million-year interval with almost no tetrapod fossils following the end-Devonian Hangenberg event, land vertebrates reappear around 345 Ma diverse and properly terrestrial, with five-digit limbs and functioning ankles.

~350 Ma — vast crinoidal carbonate platforms across Laurussia
~345 Ma — Romer's Gap ends; Pederpes and a diverse terrestrial tetrapod fauna
~340 Ma — sharks radiate; Stethacanthus and other forms with no modern analogue
~330 Ma — Gondwanan ice sheets appear; the Late Palaeozoic Ice Age begins
~325 Ma — Antler orogeny thrusts an arc onto western Laurentia

intervals.name: Late Devonian
intervals.summary: Two of the Big Five mass extinctions bracket this epoch, and it is likely that the forests caused them. Archaeopteris, the first tree with a proper woody trunk and a deep root system, spread worldwide and drove weathering rates up sharply while pumping nutrients into rivers; the resulting CO2 drawdown cooled the planet, and the nutrient flux triggered algal blooms and seafloor anoxia in the shallow seas. The Kellwasser event at the Frasnian-Famennian boundary, around 372 Ma, destroyed the great stromatoporoid-and-tabulate-coral reef systems that had been the largest reefs in Earth history — and reefs of that kind never returned. The Hangenberg event at 358.86 Ma finished the job, wiping out the armoured placoderms entirely and cutting tetrapod diversity so severely that it took 15 million years to recover. The same epoch, though, produced the single most important transition in vertebrate history: Tiktaalik at about 375 Ma with a neck and weight-bearing fins, then Acanthostega and Ichthyostega at about 365 Ma in East Greenland with recognisable limbs and digits. The first seeds appear around the same time, freeing plants from wet ground for good.
key_events: 382.31 Ma — Late Devonian begins; reefs near their all-time maximum extent
~375 Ma — Tiktaalik, a lobe-finned fish with a neck and weight-bearing fins
375-373 Ma — Kola-Dnieper and Yakutsk-Vilyui flood volcanism
372 Ma — Kellwasser event; the great Devonian reef systems collapse permanently
~365 Ma — Acanthostega and Ichthyostega: limbs with digits, East Greenland
358.86 Ma — Hangenberg event; placoderms extinct, tetrapods nearly wiped out

intervals.name: Middle Devonian
intervals.summary: The peak of the Age of Fishes and of Phanerozoic reef building. Warm shallow seas ringed Laurussia and Gondwana, and stromatoporoid sponges and tabulate corals built reef complexes larger than anything before or since — the Canning Basin of Western Australia preserves a barrier reef system hundreds of kilometres long, now standing in desert. Placoderms, armoured fish with shearing bony jaw plates rather than teeth, dominated the seas, culminating in Dunkleosteus at six metres or more with one of the most powerful bites ever measured. On land the first true forests appeared: the Gilboa fossil site in New York preserves the stumps of Eospermatopteris, tree-sized cladoxylopsids, standing where they grew at about 385 Ma, and lycopsids grew to tree size alongside them. Deep-rooting plants were already pulling CO2 down from Early Devonian levels of over 2,000 ppm. Ammonoids — the coiled cephalopods that would dominate Mesozoic seas — appear in this epoch, and it is punctuated by the Kacak and Taghanic events, which reorganised marine faunas well before the greater Late Devonian crises.
key_events: 393.47 Ma — Middle Devonian begins; Acadian orogeny building Laurussia's margin
~390 Ma — Dunkleosteus and other giant placoderms dominate the seas
~388 Ma — Kacak event disrupts marine faunas
~385 Ma — Gilboa forest, New York: the first known trees preserved in place
~385 Ma — first ammonoids appear
~384 Ma — Taghanic event; major marine faunal reorganisation

intervals.name: Early Devonian
intervals.summary: The Caledonian collision was finishing, welding Laurentia and Baltica into Laurussia — the Old Red Sandstone continent — with the Rheic Ocean still open between it and Gondwana to the south. Erosion of the fresh Caledonian mountains spread vast red alluvial plains across what is now Britain, Scandinavia, Greenland and eastern North America. CO2 was at its Devonian maximum, around 2,000 ppm, and the world was warm with no ice. This is the epoch in which land ecosystems became real rather than marginal, and one deposit shows it better than any other: the Rhynie chert of Aberdeenshire, at about 407 Ma, where hot spring silica flash-preserved an entire terrestrial community at cellular resolution — the plant Rhynia with its stomata and vascular tissue intact, plus mites, springtails, the earliest known insect, and trigonotarbid arachnids, all in growth position. In the sea, jawed fishes radiated hard, the first ammonoid ancestors appeared, and eurypterids reached their maximum size, with Jaekelopterus exceeding two and a half metres.

~415 Ma — Old Red Sandstone floodplains spread across Laurussia
~410 Ma — Jaekelopterus, a 2.5 m eurypterid, the largest arthropod known
407 Ma — Rhynie chert preserves the first complete land ecosystem in cellular detail
~400 Ma — atmospheric CO2 near 2,000 ppm; jawed fishes radiate
~395 Ma — Altay-Sayan plume volcanism in central Asia

intervals.name: Silurian
intervals.summary: A short period of recovery and conquest. The Hirnantian ice sheets melted, sea level rose, and the shallow shelves refilled — but the climate stayed unstable, and the Silurian carries a series of sharp carbon-isotope excursions each paired with a minor extinction: the Ireviken at about 433 Ma, the Mulde at about 425 and the Lau at about 424, which between them repeatedly culled the conodonts and graptolites. Tectonically, Iapetus was closing hard: Avalonia had already docked with Baltica across the Tornquist Sea, and the Scandian phase of the Caledonian orogeny around 430 Ma drove Baltica into Laurentia, raising a range whose remains are now split between Scotland, Scandinavia, Greenland and the northern Appalachians. Reefs rebuilt on a large scale. But the period's real importance is what left the water: the first unambiguous vascular land plants, Cooksonia, appear around 425 Ma — a few centimetres tall, leafless, with conducting tissue and spore capsules — and the first air-breathing land animals with them, including the millipede Pneumodesmus from Scotland. Jawed fishes became firmly established, and the eurypterids reached the peak of their diversity.
key_events: 443.1 Ma — Silurian begins; Hirnantian ice sheets melt, sea level rises
~433 Ma — Ireviken event; conodont and graptolite faunas culled
~430 Ma — Scandian collision: Baltica meets Laurentia, Caledonides rise
~425 Ma — Cooksonia, the first unambiguous vascular land plant
~425 Ma — Pneumodesmus, among the first air-breathing land animals
~424 Ma — Lau event, the last of the Silurian carbon-cycle crises

intervals.name: Late Ordovician
intervals.summary: Marine diversity reached a level it would not exceed for 200 million years, and then collapsed. Through most of the epoch the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event continued: bryozoans, articulate brachiopods, crinoids and rugose and tabulate corals filled shelf seas that flooded nearly every continent, with straight-shelled nautiloids several metres long as the top predators. Gondwana, meanwhile, was drifting over the South Pole. At about 445 Ma, with startling speed, an ice sheet grew across what is now the Sahara — glacial striations and tunnel valleys are still visible in the Algerian and Libyan desert — and sea level fell 80 to 100 metres, draining the shelves that held most of the world's marine life. The end-Ordovician extinction that followed came in two pulses, one at the glacial onset and one during the meltback, when anoxic water flooded back onto the shelves; together they removed about 85 percent of species, making this the second-largest extinction in Earth history and the only Big Five event clearly driven by cooling.
key_events: 458.2 Ma — Late Ordovician begins; diversity near its early Palaeozoic peak
~455 Ma — giant orthocone nautiloids as apex predators; first big coral reefs
450 Ma — Charlevoix and Slate Islands impacts in eastern Laurentia
446 Ma — Suordakh magmatism on the Siberian platform
445 Ma — Hirnantian glaciation; ice across Gondwanan Sahara, sea level -80 to -100 m
443.1 Ma — end-Ordovician extinction complete; ~85% of species lost in two pulses

intervals.name: Middle Ordovician
intervals.summary: The engine room of the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event, in which marine genus richness roughly tripled without any new phyla appearing — a completely different kind of radiation from the Cambrian explosion, filling out ecosystems rather than inventing body plans. Suspension-feeding tiers stacked upward from the seafloor for the first time, bryozoans and stromatoporoids built the first substantial reefs since the Cambrian archaeocyathids, and articulate brachiopods became the dominant shelly animals of the shelf. Part of the driver was climatic: the extreme heat of the Early Ordovician, with tropical sea surface temperatures above 40 C, moderated as CO2 fell, and cooler water holds more oxygen. Sea level was near its Phanerozoic maximum and continental flooding near its greatest extent. Iapetus began to close as an island arc collided with Laurentia's eastern margin in the Taconic orogeny. The oldest convincing evidence for land plants — cryptospores of liverwort grade — comes from about 470 Ma, and at 466 Ma the breakup of the L-chondrite parent body in the asteroid belt began showering Earth with meteorites for millions of years.
key_events: 471.3 Ma — Middle Ordovician begins; the biodiversification event accelerates
~470 Ma — oldest convincing land plant spores, of liverwort grade
~470 Ma — Taconic orogeny begins as an arc collides with Laurentia
466 Ma — L-chondrite parent body breaks up; a meteorite shower lasting millions of years
~465 Ma — bryozoan and stromatoporoid reefs; marine diversity triples
~460 Ma — sea level near its Phanerozoic maximum; continents at maximum flooding

intervals.name: Early Ordovician
intervals.summary: A hot, high-CO2, high-sea-level world of scattered continents: Gondwana enormous in the south, with Laurentia, Baltica and Siberia separate and Iapetus wide between them. CO2 stood at several thousand ppm and tropical sea surface temperatures probably exceeded 40 C, which appears to have actively suppressed diversity — the great Ordovician radiation does not really start until the world cools. Free oxygen was still low by later standards, only a few percent of the atmosphere. The Sauk transgression flooded Laurentia with clean quartz sand and then carbonate. Biologically the epoch is a bridge: graptolites appear near 485 Ma and become the finest zone fossils of the early Palaeozoic; conodonts diversify; the first corals and the first substantial post-Cambrian reefs appear. The Fezouata Biota of Morocco, at about 478 Ma, is the key window — a Burgess-Shale-type soft-bodied fauna showing that Cambrian oddities such as anomalocaridids and marrellomorphs survived well into the Ordovician alongside the modernising shelly fauna, rather than being swept away at the period boundary.
key_events: 486.85 Ma — Ordovician begins; Cambrian-Ordovician boundary extinctions
~485 Ma — graptolites appear and become the period's key zone fossils
~480 Ma — Sauk transgression floods Laurentia with quartz sand and carbonate
478 Ma — Fezouata Biota, Morocco: Cambrian-type soft-bodied animals in Ordovician rocks
~475 Ma — tropical sea surface temperatures above 40 C suppress diversity
~472 Ma — first corals and the first substantial post-Cambrian reefs

intervals.name: Cambrian
intervals.summary: Animals acquired hard parts, eyes and predatory ecology, and essentially every animal body plan that exists today appears in the fossil record within about 20 million years. The small shelly fauna arrives from 539 Ma, trilobites at about 521, and by 518 the Chengjiang deposits of Yunnan preserve a full marine ecosystem including Myllokunmingia, among the earliest known vertebrates; the Burgess Shale at 508 Ma preserves it again in British Columbia, with Anomalocaris as the metre-long apex predator. Land, meanwhile, was bare rock and microbial crust, with no plants of any kind. Continents were scattered: Gondwana was assembling in the south while Laurentia, Baltica and Siberia sat separately, and the Iapetus Ocean was opening between them. CO2 was extraordinarily high, perhaps 5,000 to 7,000 ppm, oxygen only a few percent, and sea level rose steadily as the Sauk transgression drowned continental interiors. Burrowing animals churned the seafloor for the first time — the agronomic revolution — ending the microbial mat-dominated world that had prevailed for three billion years. Repeated extinction pulses punctuate the period, including the SPICE carbon excursion at about 497 Ma.
key_events: 538.8 Ma — Cambrian begins; small shelly fossils and complex burrows appear
~521 Ma — first trilobites; biomineralisation becomes widespread
518 Ma — Chengjiang Biota; Myllokunmingia, among the earliest vertebrates
~510 Ma — Kalkarindji flood basalts in Australia and an extinction pulse
508 Ma — Burgess Shale; Anomalocaris and Opabinia in a fully modern food web
~497 Ma — SPICE carbon isotope excursion and trilobite extinction pulse

intervals.name: Ediacaran
intervals.summary: The first period in which the fossil record contains things you can see without a microscope. Rodinia's fragments had dispersed and Gondwana was assembling along the Pan-African and Brasiliano belts as the Mozambique Ocean closed between its eastern and western halves; by the period's end Iapetus was already opening on the other side, which is one reason the proposed supercontinent Pannotia is so contested. Climate had recovered from the Marinoan snowball, though the short Gaskiers glaciation struck at about 580 Ma, and the Shuram excursion between roughly 574 and 567 Ma is the largest negative carbon-isotope anomaly in Earth history — still without an agreed explanation. Oxygen rose. The Ediacaran biota appears in three successive assemblages: the deep-water Avalon fronds such as Charnia and Fractofusus at 575 Ma; the White Sea assemblage at about 560 Ma with Dickinsonia — whose cholesterol biomarkers confirm it as an animal — and Kimberella, which left radular scratch marks as it grazed; and the Nama assemblage at about 550 Ma, in which Cloudina and Namacalathus built the first mineralised skeletons, some already bearing predatory boreholes.
key_events: 635 Ma — Marinoan snowball ends; cap carbonates deposited worldwide
~600-550 Ma — Mozambique Ocean closes; East and West Gondwana weld together
580 Ma — Gaskiers glaciation (under 340,000 years) and the Acraman impact
575 Ma — Avalon assemblage: Charnia and Fractofusus in deep water
~574-567 Ma — Shuram excursion, the largest carbon isotope anomaly known
~550 Ma — Cloudina and Namacalathus: the first mineralised skeletons, and boreholes in them

intervals.name: Cryogenian
intervals.summary: The most extreme climate interval in the geological record, and the only period defined by glaciation. Two separate Snowball Earth events froze the planet to near-tropical latitudes: the Sturtian, from 717.4 to 661.7 Ma, which at nearly 56 million years is by far the longest glaciation known, and the Marinoan, from about 650 to 635.5 Ma. Between them lies a genuinely non-glacial interlude of some ten million years — the two events are not one continuous freeze. The trigger for the Sturtian was probably the Franklin Large Igneous Province at 719 Ma, whose fresh basalt weathered rapidly in the wet tropics and stripped CO2 from the air, compounded by Rodinia's rifting fragments sitting at low latitudes where weathering is most efficient. Escaping required the opposite extreme: with silicate weathering shut down beneath the ice, volcanic CO2 accumulated to perhaps hundreds of times modern levels before the ice gave way, and each freeze therefore ends in a super-greenhouse that precipitated the cap carbonates found on top of the tillites worldwide. Eukaryotic algae survived, and the Neoproterozoic Oxygenation Event follows the Marinoan thaw.
key_events: 720 Ma — Cryogenian begins; Rodinia rifting at low latitudes
719 Ma — Franklin Large Igneous Province erupts across Arctic Canada
717.4 Ma — Sturtian glaciation begins; ice reaches the equator
661.7 Ma — Sturtian ends after ~56 Myr, the longest glaciation known
~650 Ma — Marinoan glaciation begins after a non-glacial interlude
635.5 Ma — Marinoan ends; a super-greenhouse thaw deposits cap carbonates worldwide

intervals.name: Tonian
intervals.summary: The deep end of this timeline, and the last stretch of the long, stable, low-oxygen world sometimes called the Boring Billion. Rodinia had assembled by roughly 900 Ma along the Grenville belts, which run from Mexico through eastern Canada into Scandinavia, and it began to pull apart from about 825 Ma: the Willouran-Gairdner dykes of Australia at 827 Ma, the Guibei magmatism of South China at 822, Gunbarrel along Laurentia's edge at 780 and Mundine Well across the Pilbara at 755 all record that stretching. Climate was warm with no glaciation anywhere — the once-cited Kaigas glaciation around 750 Ma has been rejected, its type deposits reinterpreted as rift-scarp debris. CO2 stood at several thousand ppm and free oxygen at well under one percent of the atmosphere. Life was entirely microbial and single-celled, but not static: eukaryotes diversified through this period, and vase-shaped microfossils of testate amoebae from about 780 to 740 Ma provide the first clear evidence of eukaryotic predation, some specimens preserving the puncture holes where they were attacked.
key_events: 1000 Ma — Tonian begins; Rodinia assembling along the Grenville orogens
~900 Ma — Rodinia fully assembled around a Laurentian core
827 Ma — Willouran-Gairdner dykes; the first tearing of Rodinia's interior
780 Ma — Gunbarrel magmatism along Laurentia's rifting margin
~780-740 Ma — vase-shaped microfossils record the first eukaryotic predation
755 Ma — Mundine Well dykes, a key anchor for Rodinia reconstructions

supercontinents.name: Rodinia
supercontinents.summary: Rodinia assembled between roughly 1.3 and 0.9 billion years ago through the Grenvillian orogenies, a global collision system whose eroded roots can be traced from Mexico through eastern Canada into Scandinavia and on into Amazonia. Laurentia sat at the centre, ringed by Amazonia, Baltica, Kalahari, Congo, India, Siberia and the joined Australia-East Antarctica block, with the single ocean Mirovia beyond. That much is agreed; almost every detail of the fit is not, and the competing SWEAT, AUSWUS and AUSMEX reconstructions place Australia against quite different stretches of Laurentia's western margin. The interior would have been a vast, unvegetated, deeply arid rock desert, since no land plants existed to hold soil or moisture; CO2 stood at several thousand ppm, keeping the surface warm despite a Sun some six percent fainter than today, and free oxygen was well below one percent of the atmosphere. No glaciation is recorded during its coherent phase.
supercontinents.life: Entirely microbial and single-celled. Cyanobacterial mats and stromatolites dominated shallow water, though stromatolite abundance was already declining as eukaryotic grazers spread. Acritarchs — organic-walled microfossils, probably algal cysts — diversified in the plankton. The oldest taxonomically resolvable eukaryote, the red alga Bangiomorpha pubescens from Arctic Canada at about 1.05 Ga, slightly predates the supercontinent and carries the earliest evidence of sexual reproduction and of complex multicellularity. By around 780 to 740 Ma, as Rodinia was breaking apart, vase-shaped microfossils of testate amoebae record the first clear eukaryotic predation, some preserving the holes where they were bored into.
supercontinents.fate: Heat trapped beneath a supercontinent eventually undoes it, and a mantle superplume appears to have risen under Rodinia's centre. Rifting began around 825 Ma and is recorded by a sequence of large igneous provinces — Willouran-Gairdner at 827 Ma, Guibei at 822, Gunbarrel at 780, Mundine Well at 755 and finally Franklin at 719 Ma. The consequences went far beyond tectonics: the fragments were sitting at low latitudes, and enormous areas of fresh basalt weathering in the wet tropics stripped CO2 from the atmosphere fast enough to tip the planet into the Sturtian snowball at 717.4 Ma. Rodinia's breakup is therefore the leading candidate trigger for the most extreme climate event in Earth history.

supercontinents.name: Pannotia
supercontinents.summary: Pannotia — also called Greater Gondwana or the Vendian supercontinent — is the proposed latest-Precambrian mass in which Gondwana's assembling cratons were joined by Laurentia, Baltica and Siberia clustered around them, forming a V-shaped landmass around 600 Ma. Its existence as a true supercontinent is genuinely disputed in the current literature, and the app treats it as provisional. The core objection is one of timing: Gondwana's own assembly was still finishing during the Kuunga orogeny between about 570 and 530 Ma, while Laurentia was already rifting away and the Iapetus Ocean was opening from roughly 615 to 550 Ma. If one end was still docking while the other end was already leaving, there may never have been a moment when the pieces were all simultaneously joined. Palaeomagnetic data are permissive rather than conclusive, and several reconstructions allow Laurentia to have been separated from Gondwana throughout. Critics — Meert and Evans among them — argue that no more than about half of continental crust was ever assembled at once, below the usual working threshold for a supercontinent. Its defenders, Scotese most prominently, keep it as a real but very short-lived mass.
supercontinents.life: The Ediacaran biota, the first large complex organisms on Earth, lived on Pannotia's shelves. The Avalon assemblage at 575 Ma is dominated by deep-water rangeomorph fronds such as Charnia and Fractofusus with no clear modern counterpart. By about 560 Ma the White Sea assemblage adds Dickinsonia, confirmed as an animal by cholesterol biomarkers preserved in its films, and Kimberella, a mollusc-grade grazer that left paired radular scratches in the microbial mats it fed on. By 550 Ma the Nama assemblage includes Cloudina and Namacalathus, the first animals to build mineralised skeletons — and some Cloudina tubes carry predatory boreholes, the earliest direct evidence of predation on skeletal animals.
supercontinents.fate: Whatever coherence it had did not last. Iapetus and the Tornquist Sea widened, carrying Laurentia and Baltica away northward while Gondwana consolidated and drifted south; by the early Cambrian the fragments were unambiguously separate continents. The rifting is recorded by the Central Iapetus Magmatic Province between about 620 and 550 Ma. Gondwana, the piece that held, went on to survive for another 350 million years.

supercontinents.name: Gondwana
supercontinents.summary: The longest-lived large landmass of the Phanerozoic, and the one whose fossils proved continental drift. It formed as East Gondwana — India, Madagascar, Antarctica and Australia — collided with West Gondwana — South America and Africa — closing the Mozambique Ocean along the East African Orogeny between about 650 and 620 Ma, with the final welds set by the Kuunga orogeny by roughly 510 Ma. The resulting continent stretched from the equator to the South Pole and held about two thirds of the world's continental crust, its Pacific-facing margin ringed by the Ross and Terra Australis subduction belts that raised the Transantarctic Mountains. It drifted across the South Pole twice, and both times grew ice sheets: briefly and catastrophically in the Hirnantian at 445 Ma, and then for some 60 million years during the Late Palaeozoic Ice Age. The tillites and striated pavements that ice left in Brazil, South Africa, India, Australia and Antarctica make no sense on separate continents, and were among Wegener's primary arguments. Its breakup is usually dated to the interval from about 183 Ma, when the Karoo-Ferrar flood basalts split it along the line of the future Indian Ocean, to roughly 120 Ma, when Africa and South America finally parted and the South Atlantic opened. Fragments stayed in contact for far longer -- Australia did not clear Antarctica until about 35 Ma and the Drake Passage did not open until about 30 -- but by then Gondwana was not a continent, it was a set of continents that used to be one.
supercontinents.life: Gondwana's shelves hosted the Ediacaran and Cambrian radiations, and its interior later carried the Glossopteris flora — a seed fern whose tongue-shaped leaves are found across all five southern continents and nowhere else, the single most famous piece of palaeobotanical evidence for drift. The freshwater reptile Mesosaurus occurs in Permian rocks of Brazil and southern Africa and could not have crossed an ocean. Its Karoo basins preserve the finest record anywhere of the therapsids — dicynodonts, gorgonopsians and the cynodonts that led to mammals — through the end-Permian extinction and out the other side, where Lystrosaurus and Cynognathus are found from Antarctica to Russia. Later still it carried the titanosaurs, and its final fragmentation is why Madagascar, New Zealand and Australia have the isolated faunas they do.
supercontinents.fate: Gondwana was incorporated into Pangaea's southern half around 320 to 300 Ma but never lost its identity, and when Pangaea split it re-emerged as a unit before coming apart itself. The Karoo-Ferrar eruptions at 183 Ma opened the first cracks; the South Atlantic unzipped between 134 and 112 Ma, splitting the Parana-Etendeka basalt province in two; India separated from Madagascar at 88 Ma and sprinted north; Australia finally cleared Antarctica between about 85 and 45 Ma. The last severance, at the Drake Passage around 34 to 30 Ma, let the Antarctic Circumpolar Current close its loop and turned a forested continent into an ice sheet.

supercontinents.name: Laurussia (Euramerica)
supercontinents.summary: Laurussia is a minor supercontinent — perhaps a third of the world's continental crust — but it matters out of all proportion to its size, because it is where land was conquered. It formed as Iapetus closed: Avalonia rifted off Gondwana and rafted north to dock with Baltica across the Tornquist Sea, then Baltica drove into Laurentia in the Scandian collision around 430 Ma, with the Acadian phase continuing along the American margin until about 380 Ma. The Caledonian mountains it raised ran continuously from the northern Appalachians through Ireland, Scotland, Scandinavia and East Greenland — a single range now cut in half by an ocean that opened 300 million years later along almost the same line. The continent straddled the equator in a tropical to subtropical belt with a strong seasonal monsoon, and erosion off the young Caledonides spread the enormous red alluvial plains that give it its other name, the Old Red Sandstone continent.
supercontinents.life: The Old Red Sandstone rivers and floodplains hold the record of vertebrates coming ashore. The Rhynie chert of Aberdeenshire at 407 Ma preserves an entire terrestrial ecosystem in silica at cellular resolution — Rhynia with intact stomata and vascular tissue, trigonotarbid arachnids, mites, springtails and the earliest known insect. At Gilboa in New York, 385 Ma, the stumps of Eospermatopteris stand where they grew in the first known forest. The rivers held armoured fish — Cephalaspis, Bothriolepis, Dunkleosteus offshore — and at about 375 Ma Tiktaalik, with a neck and weight-bearing fins, then at 365 Ma Acanthostega and Ichthyostega in East Greenland with true limbs and digits. By 318 Ma Hylonomus, one of the first amniotes, was living inside hollow Lepidodendron stumps in Nova Scotia.
supercontinents.fate: Laurussia did not break up so much as get absorbed: Gondwana collided with it from the south in the Alleghanian and Variscan orogenies between about 340 and 280 Ma, raising the Central Pangaean Mountains and completing Pangaea, with Siberia welding on along the Urals last of all. It reappeared as a coherent block when Pangaea split, and then divided for good when the Central Atlantic opened between about 200 and 175 Ma — tearing along the Caledonian-Appalachian suture, so that the mountains Laurussia's assembly built now stand on both sides of the Atlantic.

supercontinents.name: Pangaea
supercontinents.summary: The last true supercontinent, and the only one whose geography we can reconstruct in fine detail. It was assembled by Gondwana driving north into Laurussia through the Alleghanian, Variscan and Ouachita collisions between about 340 and 280 Ma, throwing up a Himalayan-scale range along the suture, with Siberia the last major piece to attach along the closing Urals by roughly 250 Ma. The result was a C-shaped mass reaching from pole to pole, wrapped around the Tethys gulf on its eastern side with the world-ocean Panthalassa beyond. Parts of its interior lay more than 2,000 km from any coast, and the climatic consequence was extreme: a megamonsoon with violently seasonal rainfall on the margins and a continental interior so dry it produced some of the thickest evaporite and red-bed sequences in the record, including the Zechstein salt beneath the North Sea. It spans a full climate cycle, assembling during the Late Palaeozoic Ice Age and persisting through the hothouse Triassic.
supercontinents.life: Early Pangaea carried the Carboniferous coal forests — Lepidodendron and Sigillaria up to 40 metres tall — and, under about 30 percent atmospheric oxygen, arthropods of a size never repeated: the 2.5-metre Arthropleura and the dragonfly-like Meganeura — though the oxygen link is not settled, and both animals are now known from strata after the rainforest collapse that supposedly ended them. Whether the collapse then drove endemism is debated too: a 2018 re-analysis found increased cosmopolitanism instead. Gondwanan Pangaea grew Glossopteris forests. The land belonged to synapsids, first the sail-backed pelycosaurs Dimetrodon and Edaphosaurus, then the therapsids of the Karoo. Then came the end-Permian catastrophe, which killed 81 percent of marine species and every peat-forming plant lineage on the planet, leaving no coal anywhere on Earth for close to ten million years. Recovery on a single joined continent produced a strikingly uniform fauna — Lystrosaurus is found from Antarctica to Russia — and then, in the Triassic, the first dinosaurs, the first mammals, the first pterosaurs and the first turtles.
supercontinents.fate: The Central Atlantic Magmatic Province erupted at 201 Ma across what are now four continents, cracking Pangaea open along the old Appalachian-Atlas suture and driving the end-Triassic extinction in the process. Seafloor spreading started in the Central Atlantic around 170 Ma; the Karoo-Ferrar eruptions split Gondwana at 183 Ma; the South Atlantic opened from 134 Ma behind the Parana-Etendeka basalts. Its fragments have been separating ever since, and the Atlantic is still widening a few centimetres a year — which is why the next supercontinent cannot form until something stops it.

supercontinents.name: Pangaea Proxima
supercontinents.summary: Christopher Scotese's scenario, also published as Pangaea Ultima, and the one this model follows. It requires the Atlantic to develop subduction along its own margins and close: the Americas reverse course and drive back east into Africa and Europe, Africa finishes shutting the Mediterranean, and Antarctica and Australia join from the south, producing a ring-shaped continent wrapped around a landlocked remnant of the Indian Ocean by about +250 Myr. The case for it is physical rather than arbitrary: oceanic lithosphere older than roughly 180 to 200 million years becomes dense enough to founder, the oldest Atlantic crust is nearing that age, and Atlantic-facing subduction already exists at the Caribbean, Scotia and Gibraltar arcs — Duarte and colleagues argue the Gibraltar arc is actively propagating westward into Atlantic lithosphere. The case against is that the Pacific is shrinking far faster and by simple extrapolation should close first, and that mantle convection models frequently prefer continents to reconverge over the old superocean (Novopangaea) or 90 degrees away from the last supercontinent's centre (Amasia).
supercontinents.life: Unknowable, and the model makes no claim about it. What can be modelled is habitability, and the result is bleak: Farnsworth and colleagues (2023) coupled a climate model to this exact configuration and found that the combination of a supercontinent, roughly 2.5 percent higher solar luminosity, and elevated CO2 from suppressed silicate weathering gives sustained interior temperatures of 40 to 50 C, with only 8 to 16 percent of the land surface remaining within the thermal tolerance of mammals.
supercontinents.fate: Beyond the horizon of this model. On the pattern of every previous supercontinent, mantle heat trapped beneath it would eventually dome and rift it apart, on a timescale of perhaps 50 to 150 million years after assembly.

supercontinents.name: Amasia
supercontinents.summary: The scenario in which the Pacific closes rather than the Atlantic, and the continents converge over the Arctic. It comes in two flavours. Mitchell and colleagues (2012) proposed orthoversion: each supercontinent assembles roughly 90 degrees of longitude from the centre of the last one, along the ring of subduction that girdled it, which for Pangaea's successor means the Arctic. Separately, Yuan, Davies, Huang and others reached an Arctic-centred Amasia from numerical mantle convection models, in which the Pacific closes because its lithosphere is the oldest, its subduction ring already exists, and the upper mantle beneath an ageing ocean weakens over time, making it progressively easier to consume than the young, strong, subduction-free Atlantic. In favour: the Pacific genuinely is shrinking today and every piece of machinery required already exists. Against: it needs the Atlantic and Indian ridges to keep spreading indefinitely with nothing consuming their output, which is geometrically awkward on a finite sphere, and the true-polar-wander record underpinning orthoversion is contested.
supercontinents.fate: An Arctic-centred supercontinent sits at high latitude, which some climate modelling suggests would make it markedly colder and possibly glaciated at its core — a very different world from the equatorial Pangaea Proxima, and one reason the choice of scenario is not merely cosmetic.

supercontinents.name: Aurica
supercontinents.summary: Duarte and colleagues (2018) proposed the scenario in which both oceans close. New subduction invades the Atlantic — the Gibraltar arc again being the candidate seed — while the Pacific continues to be consumed at the Ring of Fire, so the continents converge from both sides; to conserve surface area a new ocean opens by rifting through Asia, roughly along the line where the Indian Ocean meets the continent. The product is an equator-centred supercontinent split by a young interior ocean, around +250 Myr. What favours it is that it takes both observed trends seriously at once rather than choosing between them, and it requires no ocean to keep spreading forever. What disfavours it is that it needs two independent, unproven events — successful Atlantic subduction invasion and the nucleation of a wholly new rift through continental Asia. Its climate is the interesting part: Way and colleagues (2021) modelled Aurica and Pangaea Ultima side by side and found Aurica several degrees cooler and substantially more habitable, because its equatorial position and interior seaway keep moisture moving across the land instead of leaving a baked continental core.
supercontinents.fate: Beyond this model's horizon. Aurica's new interior ocean would itself be a candidate to widen and take the supercontinent apart again.

supercontinents.name: Novopangaea
supercontinents.summary: The conservative scenario, and arguably the default: change nothing, invent no new plate boundaries, and simply run today's motions forward. The Pacific keeps closing at the rate it is closing now, the Atlantic keeps opening at the rate it is opening now, the Americas ride west until they meet Asia, and Antarctica drifts north to join them from the south. It is the extroversion scenario in Hoffman's terms — the continents reconverge over the old superocean rather than over the ocean that separated them — and it was popularised by Ted Nield. Its great strength is that every subduction zone it uses exists today and no new physics is required, which makes it the scenario with the fewest free parameters. Its weakness is the mirror image: it requires the Atlantic to widen indefinitely and never develop subduction, even though its oldest crust is approaching the age at which other basins have foundered, and even though Atlantic-facing arcs already exist at Gibraltar, the Caribbean and Scotia.
supercontinents.fate: Beyond this model's horizon. Because Novopangaea assembles over the closed Pacific, the succeeding breakup would be expected to reopen a basin along a quite different line from the Atlantic.
