glaciations.name: Sturtian Glaciation
glaciations.summary: The longest glaciation in Earth's history and the deeper of the two Cryogenian snowballs: ice reached the tropics and stayed for roughly 56 million years. Glacial deposits of this age are found on every continent, several of them at palaeolatitudes within a few degrees of the equator, which is the observation a merely-cold Earth cannot explain.
glaciations.cause: The Franklin large igneous province erupted across a low-latitude Rodinia at ~719 Ma. Fresh basalt weathers fast, and weathering consumes CO2 -- a continent's worth of it, sitting in the wet tropics, drew the greenhouse down until ice-albedo feedback ran away.
glaciations.end: Only volcanic CO2 could end it. With the ocean sealed and weathering stopped, CO2 accumulated for millions of years until it reached a few hundred times modern and the ice retreated catastrophically, leaving cap carbonates over the till worldwide.
glaciations.life: It brackets the interval when total-group animals were diverging: molecular clocks and the first sponge biomarkers sit around here, so the earliest animals lived through it rather than appearing after it.
glaciations.contested: Whether the ocean froze COMPLETELY (hard snowball) or kept a band of open water (slushball) is not settled. Photosynthetic life survived, which is easier to explain with refugia -- cracks, meltwater ponds, thin translucent sea ice.

glaciations.name: Marinoan Glaciation
glaciations.summary: The second Cryogenian snowball, shorter than the Sturtian at under 15 million years but reaching just as far -- ice again at sea level in the tropics. Its end is one of the sharpest events in the rock record.
glaciations.cause: Much the same machinery as the Sturtian, on a world that had not fully recovered from it. There is a genuine non-glacial interlude between the two, which is why this is a separate event and not one long freeze.
glaciations.end: Deglaciation took perhaps a few thousand years. Cap dolostones sit directly on glacial till worldwide, precipitated from an ocean flooded with weathering products under a CO2-choked atmosphere -- the record of a super-greenhouse that followed a global freezer with almost nothing in between.
glaciations.life: The Ediacaran begins at its close, at 635.5 Ma, and the first large complex organisms appear within about 60 million years of it. Whether that is cause or coincidence is one of the live questions in the field.
glaciations.contested: Duration and synchroneity are still argued over; some sections suggest the ice advanced and retreated more than once.

glaciations.name: Gaskiers Glaciation
glaciations.summary: A short, sharp Ediacaran glaciation lasting well under a million years -- and NOT a snowball. It was once counted as the third Cryogenian-style event; better dating cut it to roughly 340,000 years and showed it was regional rather than global.
glaciations.cause: Poorly constrained. It is short enough that it may not need the CO2-drawdown machinery the snowballs do.
glaciations.end: Ended as quickly as it began.
glaciations.life: The Avalon assemblage -- the first large Ediacaran organisms, the rangeomorphs of Mistaken Point -- appears in the rocks immediately above it, which is why the two keep being discussed together.
glaciations.contested: Its extent, and whether it has any causal relationship with the Avalon radiation at all.

glaciations.name: Andean-Saharan Glaciation
glaciations.summary: The Palaeozoic's first great icehouse, centred on Gondwana as it drifted over the South Pole. Its peak, the Hirnantian, was brief -- perhaps a million years -- but it dropped global sea level by around 100 metres and drained the shallow tropical shelves where almost all life then lived.
glaciations.cause: Gondwana's arrival at the pole gave ice somewhere to grow. Falling CO2 through the Ordovician, helped by the weathering of the newly raised Taconic mountains and possibly by the first land plants, did the rest.
glaciations.end: The ice melted within a couple of million years, seas rose, and oxygen-poor water spread back over the shelves.
glaciations.life: It drove the End-Ordovician mass extinction, the only one of the big five caused by cold: about 85% of marine species, in two pulses -- the first from the draining shelves, the second from the anoxia that came with the meltwater.
glaciations.contested: Whether ice persisted at lower intensity through the Silurian, and how much the spread of early land plants contributed to the CO2 drawdown.

glaciations.name: Late Devonian Glaciation
glaciations.summary: A late Famennian icehouse pulse on high-latitude Gondwana, recorded by diamictites and striated pavements across Bolivia, Peru and Brazil. Shorter and smaller than the ice ages either side of it, and easy to overlook -- this app did not show it at all until recently.
glaciations.cause: The Devonian is when forests took over the land. Deep-rooted trees weather rock far faster than anything before them, and burying their carbon pulled CO2 down hard -- the same greening that made the world habitable made it cold.
glaciations.end: Gave way to the warmth of the earliest Carboniferous before the far larger Late Palaeozoic Ice Age began.
glaciations.life: It sits within the drawn-out Late Devonian extinctions, alongside the Kellwasser and Hangenberg events, and cooling is one of the mechanisms usually invoked for them.
glaciations.contested: Its extent is much less constrained than the Hirnantian or the LPIA; estimates of ice volume vary widely.

glaciations.name: Late Palaeozoic Ice Age
glaciations.summary: The longest icehouse of the Phanerozoic -- some eighty million years -- and the only one whose ice volume matched or exceeded the last glacial maximum. Ice covered high-latitude Gondwana across what is now South America, southern Africa, India, Australia and Antarctica, and it waxed and waned in cycles driven by the same orbital rhythms that drove the Pleistocene.
glaciations.cause: Coal. Carboniferous swamp forests buried organic carbon on a scale never repeated, while Gondwana sat over the South Pole and the rising Central Pangaean Mountains weathered fast. CO2 fell and oxygen rose to the highest levels in Earth's history.
glaciations.end: Ended in the Permian as Pangaea's assembly dried the interior, the coal forests collapsed, and CO2 climbed again.
glaciations.life: Its glacial-interglacial cycles drove the rainforest collapse of the Late Carboniferous, fragmenting the coal forests into refugia and pushing tetrapods toward the fully terrestrial amniote way of life. Whether those refugia then bred endemism is not settled: the classic reading says each island evolved its own fauna, and a 2018 re-analysis found increased cosmopolitanism instead. The collapse itself is Euramerican -- the Cathaysian rainforests of South China carry on to the end-Permian.
glaciations.contested: Whether it was one continuous ice age or a series of discrete glacial episodes separated by ice-free intervals. The evidence increasingly favours the second.

glaciations.name: Early Cretaceous Cool Snap
glaciations.summary: A cool interval in the middle of a hothouse world, and the most contested entry here. Glendonites -- a mineral that forms only near freezing -- and scattered dropstones in Australia and the Arctic point to high-latitude ice, but no continental ice sheet is accepted for the Cretaceous.
glaciations.cause: Not resolved. A dip in volcanic CO2 output is the usual suggestion.
glaciations.end: Whatever ice there was is gone by the mid-Cretaceous, the hottest sustained interval of the last 200 million years.
glaciations.life: Nothing is attributed to it. Dinosaurs at high latitudes lived through polar winters regardless of ice.
glaciations.contested: Everything about it, including whether it happened. It is shown here as small polar ice rather than left out, because the field evidence is real even where its interpretation is disputed.

glaciations.name: Late Cenozoic Ice Age
glaciations.summary: The icehouse we are still in. It began when Antarctica glaciated at the Eocene-Oligocene boundary in under 100,000 years, and it is the only ice age whose full course this map can follow -- from a single southern ice sheet to the bipolar world of the last three million years.
glaciations.cause: Falling CO2 through the Cenozoic, the opening of the Drake and Tasman gateways that let the Antarctic Circumpolar Current isolate the south, and the uplift of the Himalaya and Tibet accelerating silicate weathering.
glaciations.end: It has not ended. We are in an interglacial, and orbital forcing alone would have brought another glacial in tens of thousands of years -- though the CO2 already released has probably deferred that.
glaciations.life: Its cycles built the modern biosphere: the mammoth steppe, the repeated opening and closing of land bridges, the isolation and reconnection of populations that drove so much recent speciation, and the ice-free corridors that shaped where people went.
glaciations.contested: The trigger for Northern Hemisphere glaciation at ~2.7 Ma, and the cause of the mid-Pleistocene shift from 41,000 to 100,000-year cycles.

glaciations.name: Baykonurian Glaciation
glaciations.summary: A terminal-Ediacaran glaciation that most compilations leave out, recorded by diamictites in Kazakhstan, Iran, Baltica and elsewhere. It sits in the last few million years of the Precambrian and was nothing like a snowball — its extent is poorly constrained and no one claims tropical ice.
glaciations.cause: Not established. It follows the long Ediacaran warm interval and precedes the Cambrian carbon-isotope excursions, and no trigger has been agreed.
glaciations.end: It ends just before the Cambrian boundary; the boundary itself carries no glacial deposits.
glaciations.life: It overlaps the disappearance of the Ediacaran biota, which makes it a candidate contributor to that turnover — though the case is not made, and competing explanations (bioturbation, predation, oceanic chemistry) do not need it.
glaciations.contested: Moderate confidence overall. Correlation between the scattered diamictite occurrences is the weak point: they are dated well enough to be terminal Ediacaran and not well enough to be proved synchronous.

climate_events.name: Palaeocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum
climate_events.summary: The fastest large warming in the geological record, and the closest thing deep time offers to a controlled experiment on our own. Somewhere between 3,000 and 7,000 billion tonnes of carbon entered the ocean–atmosphere system in roughly 20,000 years, and global mean temperature rose 5–8 °C.
climate_events.cause: Unresolved, and worth saying so. The North Atlantic Igneous Province, erupting through organic-rich sediment as the Atlantic opened, is the leading candidate; destabilised methane hydrate and thawing high-latitude permafrost are the others. The carbon's isotopic signature says it was biological in origin, which narrows it without settling it.
climate_events.end: About 200,000 years, and that number is the one worth remembering: the release was fast, the recovery was not. Silicate weathering and organic burial drew the carbon back down on their own schedule, which is the schedule the Earth system has.
climate_events.life: The deep sea acidified sharply enough to dissolve carbonate on the sea floor, and benthic foraminifera suffered their largest extinction of the Cenozoic. On land, mammals responded by getting small, and the modern orders — primates, artiodactyls, perissodactyls — appear almost at once and spread across the northern continents. The Arctic Ocean reached sea-surface temperatures a swimmer would call warm.
climate_events.contested: The source of the carbon, and therefore how fast it can have been released. Estimates of the injection rate differ by an order of magnitude, which is exactly the quantity a comparison with the present turns on.

climate_events.name: Azolla Event
climate_events.summary: For about 800,000 years the Arctic Ocean was a freshwater pond covered in fern. Continental positions had left the basin almost cut off, and high evaporation plus river discharge stacked a fresh layer on top of dense salt water — deep enough for Azolla, a floating fern, to colonise the whole surface.
climate_events.cause: Under twenty hours of daylight and a very high CO₂ sky, Azolla can double its biomass in two or three days, fixing roughly a tonne of nitrogen and removing about six tonnes of carbon per acre per year. Over four million square kilometres and 800,000 years that is enough on its own to account for an 80% fall in atmospheric CO₂ — from about 3,500 ppm in the early Eocene to about 650 ppm.
climate_events.end: The Arctic's connection to the world ocean reopened as the plates moved, salt water returned, and the fern died out of the basin. What it had already removed did not come back.
climate_events.life: Arctic sea-surface temperatures fell from around 13 °C toward the freezing values of today, and for the first time in more than 500 million years the planet could carry ice at both poles. This is the moment greenhouse Earth begins turning into the icehouse we live in — and the agent was a pond weed.
climate_events.contested: Moderate confidence. The deposit is not in doubt — an eight-metre-plus unit in the ACEX Arctic cores, alternating marine silica with millimetre laminae of fossil Azolla, correlated basin-wide by a gamma-ray spike — but the magnitude of the drawdown attributable to it is debated.

climate_events.name: Early Eocene Climatic Optimum
climate_events.summary: The warmest sustained interval of the Cenozoic and the top of the long Palaeogene greenhouse: crocodilians and palms in the Arctic, no permanent ice anywhere, and the pole-to-equator temperature gradient at its flattest. Everything after it is, on average, downhill — the EECO is where the 50-million-year cooling that produced the modern world begins.
climate_events.cause: Sustained high CO₂ — of order 1,400–1,700 ppm — from a combination of North Atlantic volcanism and slow weathering under a world with little exposed fresh silicate rock at high latitude.
climate_events.end: Not an event but a turn. Weathering caught up, the Azolla event and the opening of the Southern Ocean gateways pulled carbon and heat out of the system, and by 34 Ma there was ice on Antarctica.
climate_events.life: A flat temperature gradient means a world with no real climate zones as we know them; forests ran to both poles and the tropics were not much warmer than the mid-latitudes.
climate_events.contested: Two smaller warm reversals interrupt the long cooling and are worth knowing about: the Middle Eocene Climatic Optimum (MECO, ~40.5–40 Ma, a 4–6 °C rebound in the middle of the decline) and the Mid-Miocene Climatic Optimum (MMCO, ~17–14 Ma), the last time the world was reliably warmer than today.

climate_events.name: Oceanic Anoxic Event 2
climate_events.summary: At the hottest moment of the last 200 million years, the deep ocean ran out of oxygen. A warm ocean holds less oxygen, mixes less, and was being fed nutrients by a hyperactive hydrological cycle; productivity bloomed, the organic rain stripped what oxygen was left, and for roughly 820,000 years the sea floor across much of the world accumulated black, finely laminated mud with no burrows in it at all — no animal could live there to disturb it.
climate_events.cause: Almost certainly the Caribbean and Madagascar large igneous provinces, erupting at the right moment and delivering both CO₂ and the trace metals that fertilise a bloom.
climate_events.end: The burial of all that organic carbon is itself the fix: it draws CO₂ down, the ocean cools and re-ventilates. Around 70% of the world's oil source rocks are Mesozoic, and events like this are why.
climate_events.life: A sharp turnover among planktonic foraminifera and radiolaria, and the extinction of much of the deep-water benthos over the affected basins.
climate_events.contested: How this looked is worth being careful about, because it is easy to draw wrongly. Anoxia is a SUBSURFACE condition: the Black Sea is completely oxygen-free below about 100 m today and its surface looks entirely ordinary. The Cretaceous ocean was not green or purple; it was blue, over a dead floor — which is why this app renders anoxia in the sediment and never in the water colour. On temperature: PhanDA puts the Turonian global mean near 36 °C, the Phanerozoic maximum; this app's curve sits between PhanDA and Scotese and reads 33 °C here.

climate_events.name: Oceanic Anoxic Event 1a
climate_events.summary: The earlier of the two great Cretaceous anoxic events, lasting about 1.0–1.3 million years, and the one with the clearest trigger of any of them.
climate_events.cause: The Ontong Java Plateau — the largest volcanic edifice on Earth, 1.86 million km² of sea floor built in a few million years. The carbon-isotope record swings hard at exactly its eruption.
climate_events.end: The same negative feedback as OAE 2: organic burial removes the carbon that caused it.
climate_events.life: Calcareous nannoplankton suffered a sharp crisis — a nannoconid decline that is one of the event's diagnostic markers.
climate_events.contested: Two smaller companions belong on the same shelf: OAE 1b (Paquier), in the Albian, and OAE 3, Coniacian–Santonian and more regional than global. Whether OAE 3 counts as an ocean anoxic event at all is argued.

climate_events.name: Hirnantian Anoxia
climate_events.summary: The second pulse of the End-Ordovician extinction, and the mechanism behind it. The first pulse was the glaciation itself — sea level fell, the shelf seas that held most of the world's animals drained away. The second was what came back: as the ice melted, anoxic water spread over the shelves that had just been re-flooded.
climate_events.cause: A stratified, warming ocean over newly flooded shelves, with nutrients delivered by the deglaciation. The same sequence as the Cretaceous events, run in reverse order — cold first, then anoxia.
climate_events.end: With the ice gone and circulation restored, the shelves re-ventilated. The recovery fauna is markedly different from what went in.
climate_events.life: Together the two pulses removed about 85% of marine species, the second-largest extinction in the record. Graptolites, trilobites and brachiopods all took heavy losses.
climate_events.contested: The relative weight of cooling, sea-level fall and anoxia in the total kill is still argued, and metal poisoning has been proposed as a fourth agent.

climate_events.name: Great Oxidation Event
climate_events.summary: The single largest change in Earth's surface chemistry — and it happened long before this map begins, which is why it is listed here rather than drawn. Free oxygen went from about 0.001% of today's level to a few percent.
climate_events.cause: Oxygenic photosynthesis had existed for a long time before this; what changed was that the sinks — dissolved iron, volcanic gases, unweathered crust — were finally saturated. Oxygen accumulates only once there is nothing left to consume it.
climate_events.end: It was not a smooth ramp. Oxygen overshot to near modern levels around 2.3 Ga (the Lomagundi–Jatuli excursion) and crashed again at 2.1 Ga, after which it stayed low for more than a billion years.
climate_events.life: Everything followed from it. Methane, the greenhouse gas holding the Archaean warm, was oxidised away and the planet froze into the Huronian glaciation. Banded iron formations, which need a deep ocean full of dissolved iron, largely stopped forming by 1.85 Ga; red beds appeared; an ozone layer formed, and the strange sulfur-isotope chemistry of an unshielded atmosphere disappeared from the record. Anaerobic life was mass-extinguished — the biosphere may have contracted by more than 80%. And more than 2,500 of Earth's roughly 4,500 mineral species owe their existence to it.
climate_events.contested: The timing of the rise is better constrained than its shape, and whether there were earlier transient 'whiffs' of oxygen — several are claimed back to 3.0 Ga — is actively argued.
